documents.scope: Entry point, crawl root, and routing map. Corpus scope: The Networked MPLPB corpus format: seeds, validation, replication, network routing, provenance
documents.text:
Main Index — Networked MPLPB Reference Seed Boot block What this corpus is. The reference seed for Networked MPLPB. It contains nothing but the rules for being a seed: how to open it, verify it, copy it, declare what the copy is, validate it, and join a network. Every other corpus in the reference experiment grows from a copy of this directory. Authoritative root. This file. Every internal link is
relative to it. The crawl boundary is this directory; a link resolving outside
it must be rejected. Identity. This corpus is identified by the corpus ID in _net/ , not by where it is stored or which
machine serves it. Copying it does not copy any machine's identity. Retrieval rule. Answer corpus-dependent questions from
retrieved pages. Prefer status: current pages reachable from this
index. Cite a page by corpus ID, document ID, version, and status. Routing. A router decides where an answer should come from;
it does not write the answer. If a question belongs to another corpus, say
which. If several corpora plausibly own it, report the ambiguity. If the owner
is known but unreachable, say so; never impersonate it. Provenance. Anything retrieved from another corpus keeps
that corpus's identity. Transport is not authorship. Discovery is not
authority. Caching is not authorship. Change. Pages are superseded, never silently overwritten.
Retired versions live in _log/superseded/ . A corpus may only
supersede its own documents. How to make another working copy. See spec/seed.html . The rules this corpus must
satisfy are written out in plain language in spec/validation.html , so they can be
re-implemented without the software that wrote them. Category map Specification & Network Rules scope: how this corpus is built, copied, validated, routed, and cited Corpus Identity scope: corpus ID, declared scope, vocabulary, lineage, manifest Revision log scope: append-only record of changes and supersessions

documents.scope: Routing by declared scope, provenance envelopes, origin depth, supersession across corpora
documents.text:
Network Rules Routing Each corpus declares a scope and a list of scope terms drawn from its
vocabulary. A router scores known corpora by how many query terms (and their
declared synonyms) appear in each scope. One clear leader owns the query.
Several close leaders are reported as ambiguous , with their lineage,
and are never merged. No match is reported as not found in known
network . A known owner that cannot be reached is reported as unavailable ; the router does not substitute another corpus's answer.
A byte-identical mirror of the same corpus ID may serve in its place, and the
citation still names both the corpus and the machine that served it. Provenance envelope Every retrieved page travels with: corpus ID, document ID, version, status,
origin, origin depth, content hash, the corpus fingerprint, the serving node,
and the route it took. The content hash must appear in the corpus manifest;
the fingerprint must appear in the serving node's signed description. A relay
or cache may add an attestation that it relayed the page. It may not change
who wrote it. Origin depth A human-authored page has depth 0. An unratified machine-produced page has
depth 1 or more. A page derived from others has depth one greater than the
deepest of them. Copying machine text verbatim does not reset depth; only a
recorded ratification ( ratified-by , ratified-at )
does, and the ratification travels with the page. Depth is not truth. It is
derivational distance. Each node chooses its own maximum depth to serve. Supersession across corpora A corpus may supersede only its own documents. A descendant that disagrees
with its source records diverges-from , not supersedes . The source's page stays the source's page.

documents.scope: How to turn this directory into another working corpus or node without the original author
documents.text:
Instantiating a Copy This page is written for a reader who has a copy of this directory and
nothing else: no author, no original machine, possibly no software from the
project at all. 1. Open it Open index.html in any browser. Every link is relative, so the
directory can live anywhere. 2. Check it is intact _net/manifest.json lists every file with its SHA-256 hash.
Compute the SHA-256 of each listed file with any tool you have
( sha256sum , shasum -a 256 , certutil ) and
compare. The corpus fingerprint is the SHA-256 of the file list written as
compact JSON with sorted keys. A file that is present but not listed, or
listed but different, means the copy is not the corpus it claims to be. 3. Decide what the copy is A byte-identical copy is a mirror : same corpus ID, same
fingerprint, nothing to change. If you intend to add or change anything, the
copy becomes a new corpus and must say so: descendant — a new corpus seeded from this one, owning a
new domain; fork — a new corpus that continues this one's domain under
separate governance; partial — a new corpus carrying only some spokes. In all three cases: give it a new corpus ID in _net/corpus.json , set relation , record seeded_from (the old corpus ID and fingerprint), and append an
event to _net/lineage.json whose prev field is the
SHA-256 of the previous event. Seeded-from is lineage, not endorsement. 4. Make it a node A node is a machine that carries one or more corpora and publishes a small
signed description of them. The description lives outside every corpus, so a
copied corpus never carries a machine's identity. See Network Rules . 5. Validate The rules are in Validation Rules . The
reference tool is python3 -m mplpb_net validate <dir> , but
nothing in the rules depends on it.

documents.scope: Every structural check a copy must pass, stated in plain language
documents.text:
Validation Rules These are the structural rules a copy of this corpus must satisfy. They are
written so that someone could re-implement them in any language, decades from
now, without the program that first enforced them. Passing them means the
corpus is well-formed. It does not mean anything in it is true. 11.1 — Link validity Every link from one page of the corpus to another file of the corpus is relative and points at a file that exists. Failure mode: FM-L1. 11.2 — Root reachability Every page that is not a retired page can be reached by following links from index.html. Failure mode: FM-L2. 11.3 — Required metadata Every page declares document-id, category, updated, scope, when-to-use and status as mplpb meta tags; status is current or retired; every page except index.html has a rel=index link and a rel=up link. Failure mode: FM-L3. 11.4 — Unique identity No two current pages share a document ID. 11.5 — Supersession consistency Retired pages live under _log/superseded/ and nowhere else; pages there are retired; every supersedes value names a retired page; no navigation index links a retired page. Failure mode: FM-L6. 11.6 — Boundary safety No link resolves to a location outside the corpus directory. Failure mode: FM-L4. 11.7 — Index consistency Every current page is listed in its spoke's _index.html, or in index.html if it belongs to no spoke. 11.8 — Timestamp format Every updated value is an ISO 8601 time with a timezone, a space, and a version token such as v3. Failure mode: FM-L9. N.1 — Corpus identity _net/corpus.json exists and declares protocol, corpus_id, title, kind, scope, scope_terms, relation and seeded_from; relation is origin, descendant, fork or partial; anything but origin names the corpus ID and fingerprint it was seeded from; _net/_index.html repeats the corpus ID and carries the SHA-256 of corpus.json so the human twin cannot silently disagree with the machine file. Failure mode: FM-N14. N.2 — Manifest integrity _net/manifest.json lists every file in the corpus except itself with its SHA-256; every hash matches; no file is unlisted; manifest_sha256 is the SHA-256 of the file list written as compact JSON with sorted keys. Failure mode: FM-N12. N.3 — Lineage chain _net/lineage.json is a list of events numbered from 0; each event's prev field is the SHA-256 of the previous event as compact sorted JSON (empty for the first); the last event names this corpus's ID. Failure mode: FM-N12. N.4 — Declared scope The corpus declares a non-empty scope sentence and at least one scope term, and every scope term appears in _net/vocabulary.json. Failure mode: FM-N1. N.5 — No machine identity inside The corpus contains no node description, key file, or configuration: those belong to the machine carrying it, so copying the corpus never copies a machine's identity. Failure mode: FM-N14. N.6 — Scoped supersession A supersedes value may only name a document in this corpus. A page that departs from another corpus's document says so with diverges-from. Failure mode: FM-N6. N.7 — Origin depth origin is human, machine or ratified; human and ratified pages have depth 0; machine pages have depth 1 or more and at least one greater than any local page they are derived from; a ratified page names who ratified it and when. Failure mode: FM-N7. N.8 — Seed completeness The corpus carries what a stranger needs: index.html with a boot block, BOOT.md, spec/seed.html, spec/validation.html, _log/revisions.html and every _net file, so a copy can instantiate another copy without asking anyone. Failure mode: FM-N10.
